# Introduction

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
*Authors: Nataliia (source bias & Germany analysis), Anna (data structure & US analysis), Camille (worldwide distribution)*
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
*— Nataliia*
:::

This report analyses the GlobalGeoTree dataset, a global collection of approximately 6 million georeferenced tree observations covering species, taxonomic groups, and geographical locations of trees collected by diverse groups across the world. The goal is to understand how the dataset was assembled, what biases it contains, and how tree recording patterns vary across time, geography, and data sources.

GlobalGeoTree aggregates tree observations from a large number of independent sources: citizen-science platforms, institutional herbarium and museum collections, systematic field inventories, compiled floristic atlases, and various research and conservation projects. The loaded dataset covers observations from 2015 to 2024.

Because GlobalGeoTree is assembled from many independent sources, it does not reflect a systematic global sampling design — it reflects where people happened to record trees. The result is a dataset with strong geographic, taxonomic, and temporal biases that are source-driven rather than biologically meaningful. Understanding these biases is a prerequisite for any downstream analysis. To make the source structure interpretable, each observation's free-text source name is classified into one of seven groups using keyword matching (see the Methodology section for details and limitations).

The report is organised in three parts. **Part I** examines global patterns: which sources dominate the dataset and how they shape what we see, how observations have changed over time, and how taxonomic composition and species richness vary across the world. **Part II** zooms into Germany as a whole and then Berlin in detail. Baden-Württemberg and NRW appear only through selected density and NUTS3 district maps that provide visual context for interpreting Berlin. **Part III** examines the United States, the most-represented country in the dataset, analysing species composition and geographic patterns at the national level.

All charts in this report show **recording intensity** — how many observations were recorded and where — not a direct census of trees. High values can reflect actual tree presence, but they equally reflect where observers and platforms are most active.

```{r helpers-and-classify}
#| include: false
# ── Report-wide helper functions ──────────────────────────────────────────────
format_number <- function(x) {
  scales::comma(x, accuracy = 1)
}

format_percent <- function(x) {
  scales::percent(x, accuracy = 0.1)
}

nice_table <- function(data, caption = NULL) {
  knitr::kable(data, caption = caption, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
}

sample_up_to <- function(data, n_max) {
  if (nrow(data) <= n_max) {
    return(data)
  }
  set.seed(map_sample_seed)
  dplyr::slice_sample(data, n = n_max)
}

valid_map_points <- function(data) {
  data |>
    filter(
      !is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude),
      between(latitude, -90, 90), between(longitude, -180, 180)
    )
}

empty_plot <- function(message) {
  ggplot() +
    annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = message, size = 4) +
    theme_void()
}

# ── classify_source() ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Assigns each raw source name to one of seven groups.
# Rules are applied in order — the first matching condition wins.
classify_source <- function(x) {
  x_lower <- str_to_lower(str_trim(x))
  case_when(
    str_detect(x_lower, "^(unknown( source)?|missing|n/?a|na|none|null|^$)$") ~ "Other / unknown",

    str_detect(x_lower, "inaturalist|inat")    ~ "iNaturalist",
    str_detect(x_lower, "plantnet|pl@ntnet")   ~ "Pl@ntNet",
    str_detect(x_lower, "gbif")                ~ "GBIF (aggregator)",

    str_detect(x_lower,
      paste0(
        "artportalen|artdatabanken|artsdatabanken|",
        "species observation service|",
        "observation\\.org|waarnemingen|observations\\.be|natagora|",
        "naturgucker|artenfinder|",
        "irecord|bsbi recording|",
        "naturemapr|ozatlas|",
        "laji\\.fi|laji |",
        "arter\\.dk|naturbasen|",
        "flora\\.pt|",
        "inpn|faune-|",
        "species sightings|bioblitz"
      )
    ) ~ "Other citizen-science apps",

    str_detect(x_lower,
      paste0(
        "herbar|museum|botanic|arboretum|",
        "natural history|national collection|herbier national|",
        "inventory|inventaire|census|survey|monitoring|",
        "forest inventory|inventaire forestier|",
        "permanent plot|tree plot|transect|woodland survey|tree register|",
        "classified forest|conservation|protected area|",
        "parc national|national park|",
        "naturalists.? society|ornithological society|",
        "biofokus|onab|for[eê]t de lama|",
        "woody species|wild food plants|",
        "rewilding|reforestation|afforestation|tree planting"
      )
    ) ~ "Institutional & survey data",

    str_detect(x_lower,
      paste0(
        "atlas|flora |floristic|vascular plant|",
        "databank|biodiversit[aä]tsdatenbank|",
        "bsbi|bionet|kastikka|florus|",
        "\\bbien\\b|rainbio|",
        "plants of the world|world checklist|world flora|",
        "tropicos|checklist of|flora of "
      )
    ) ~ "Reference & thematic databases",
    str_detect(x_lower, "wikidata|wikipedia") ~ "Reference & thematic databases",
    str_detect(x_lower,
      "non-native|non native|invasive|alien species|alien plant|weed|biosecurity|exotique"
    ) ~ "Reference & thematic databases",
    str_detect(x_lower,
      paste0(
        "impacto ambiental|estudio de impacto|proyecto|",
        "hidroel[eé]ctrico|interconexi[oó]n|l[ií]nea de transmisi[oó]n|",
        "gasoducto|embalse|plan de manejo|restauraci[oó]n|",
        "minera|aprovechamiento forestal"
      )
    ) ~ "Reference & thematic databases",

    TRUE ~ "Other / unknown"
  )
}
```

# Methodology

This section summarises the analytical choices that the code implements. It provides context for interpreting the results without requiring the reader to examine every code block.

**Data scope.** The loaded GlobalGeoTree observation file covers the period 2015–2024. Rows with missing country codes or missing species names are removed during loading. The remaining records form the working dataset for the global, Germany, and US analyses.

**Source classification.** Each observation carries a free-text source field with thousands of distinct values. A keyword-matching function (`classify_source()`) assigns each source name to one of seven groups: iNaturalist, Pl\@ntNet, Other citizen-science apps, GBIF (aggregator), Institutional & survey data, Reference & thematic databases, and Other / unknown. The rules are applied in order, and the first match wins. This approach works well for English-language source names and major platforms but can misclassify source names in other languages or those using project-specific abbreviations. The "Other / unknown" group is a catch-all for everything that did not match any rule.

**Geographic boundaries.** For the Germany analysis, administrative boundaries at the NUTS1 level (Bundesländer) and NUTS3 level (districts) are loaded from GISCO, the geographic information system of the European Commission. Berlin district boundaries come from a separate open-data project. If a local copy of these files exists, it is used directly; otherwise the file is downloaded from the public URL on first render.

**Visualisation choices.** Maps with individual observation points use reproducible random subsamples for readability and to keep the PDF size manageable (see below). Aggregate charts, counts, richness tables, rarefaction analyses, and source-analysis summaries always use the full relevant data. English common names for species are fetched from the GBIF API and cached locally.

**Subsampling strategy.** The full dataset contains over 6 million observations. Rendering every row as an individual map point is prohibitively slow and produces visually indistinguishable results compared to a well-chosen subsample. All point maps in this report therefore use reproducible random subsampling (fixed seed 42) via a `sample_up_to()` helper, which returns all rows when the data is smaller than the requested cap. Worldwide non-source point maps draw up to 40,000 observations (per facet where applicable). Source-analysis maps draw up to 50,000 per source group. Density maps (kernel density estimation) also draw up to 50,000 observations, as KDE smoothing is stable well below this threshold. US maps follow the same approach with US-specific caps. Germany maps use smaller region-specific caps, though the German subset is small enough that most caps are not reached and all available observations are displayed. Crucially, all analytical summaries — counts, rankings, richness calculations, and rarefaction analyses — use the complete, unsampled data.

**Reading density maps.** Several maps in this report use smooth filled density contours (2D kernel density estimation) to highlight where observations are most concentrated. The legend shows contour levels from low to high: darker or more saturated colours indicate areas where more observations are clustered per unit area. These are *relative* density levels within each individual map — the same level number on two different maps does not imply the same absolute observation count. As with all maps in this report, density maps show *recording intensity*, not true tree abundance.

# Part I: Global Patterns {.unnumbered}

# Data Preparation

## Data Loading and Cleaning

The raw CSV is read with `fread()` for speed. String fields are trimmed, numeric columns are type-cast, and rows with missing country codes or species names are removed. Each observation's free-text source name is classified into one of seven source groups (see Methodology). Continent labels are derived by spatially joining observation coordinates to a world countries shapefile, with manual corrections for Russia (split at 60°E) and Réunion (reassigned to Africa).

```{r load-and-clean}
#| cache: true
raw <- fread(observations_path, showProgress = FALSE)

df <- raw |>
  mutate(
    source_raw   = ifelse(
      is.na(source) | str_trim(source) == "",
      "unknown source",
      str_trim(source)
    ),
    source_group = factor(classify_source(source_raw), levels = source_group_levels),
    country_code = str_to_upper(str_trim(country_code)),
    level3_species = str_trim(level3_species),
    level1_family  = str_trim(level1_family),
    level2_genus   = str_trim(level2_genus),
    year      = as.integer(year),
    latitude  = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(latitude)),
    longitude = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(longitude))
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(country_code), country_code != "",
    !is.na(level3_species), level3_species != ""
  )

rm(raw)
```

```{r continent-assignment}
#| cache: true
points <- st_as_sf(df,
                   coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
                   crs = 4326)

world <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")

points_continent <- st_join(points, world["continent"])

df$continent <- points_continent$continent
rm(points, points_continent)

df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    continent = case_when(
      location == "Russian Federation" & longitude < 60 ~ "Europe",
      location == "Russian Federation" & longitude >= 60 ~ "Asia",
      location == "Réunion" & latitude < -20 ~ "Africa",
      TRUE ~ continent
    )
  )

df <- df[!is.na(df$continent), ]
df <- df[df$continent != "Seven seas (open ocean)", ]

data <- df

df_world_map_base <- valid_map_points(df)

df_world_map_sample <- sample_up_to(df_world_map_base, world_map_sample_n)

df_world_map_sample_by_level0 <- df_world_map_base |>
  filter(!is.na(level0), level0 != "") |>
  group_by(level0) |>
  group_modify(~ sample_up_to(.x, world_map_sample_n)) |>
  ungroup()

df_world_map_sample_by_period <- df_world_map_base |>
  mutate(
    periode = case_when(
      year %in% c(2015, 2016) ~ "2015–2016",
      year %in% c(2017, 2018) ~ "2017–2018",
      year %in% c(2019, 2020) ~ "2019–2020",
      year %in% c(2021, 2022) ~ "2021–2022",
      year %in% c(2023, 2024) ~ "2023–2024"
    ),
    periode = factor(periode, levels = period_levels)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(periode)) |>
  group_by(periode) |>
  group_modify(~ sample_up_to(.x, world_map_sample_n)) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r data-summary}
data_summary <- tibble(
```

## Dataset Overview

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
*— Anna*
:::

| Column | Description |
|----|----|
| `sample_id` | Entry ID |
| `country_code` | Code of the country (e.g. US for the USA) |
| `level0` | Broad vegetation category grouping plants by shared ecological and physiological traits (e.g. Evergreen Broadleaf) |
| `level1_family` | Taxonomic Family — a group of related genera sharing common evolutionary characteristics (e.g. Asphodelaceae) |
| `level2_genus` | Taxonomic Genus — a group of closely related species (e.g. Aloe) |
| `level3_species` | Taxonomic Species — the most specific classification level (e.g. Aloe africana) |
| `location` | Country name |
| `source` | Source from which the occurrence record was obtained (e.g. iNaturalist Research-grade Observations) |
| `species_key` | Species identifier |
| `year` | Year of the observation |
| `longitude` | Geographic longitude |
| `latitude` | Geographic latitude |

## Distribution of the data across the world

Data distribution across the different countries:

```{r}
# Count for each country
country_counts <- data %>% count(country_code, sort = TRUE)
# Histogram of the 20 first countries only

country_counts %>% slice_max(n, n = 20) %>% ggplot(aes(x = reorder(country_code, n), y = n)) + geom_col(fill = "steelblue") + coord_flip() + labs( x = "Country", y = "Number of observations", title = "20 most represented countries" )
```

We see that most of the data come from developed western countries, and especially the US that have a very important number of observations compared to the other countries.

Yearly distribution of the data in different countries: is there any evolution of the data collected throughout the years? Do some countries present large imbalance in the data distribution? How could this affect our analysis?

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
top20_countries <- data %>% count(country_code, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = 20)

# Counting of every data for each country per year count(country_code, year)
country_year_counts <- data %>%
  filter(country_code %in% top20_countries$country_code) %>%
  count(country_code, year)

# Order the years : recent -> old
country_year_counts$year <- factor(
  country_year_counts$year,
  levels = sort(unique(country_year_counts$year), decreasing = TRUE)
)

ggplot(country_year_counts, aes(x = reorder(country_code, n, FUN = sum), y = n, fill = year)) + geom_col() + coord_flip() + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired") + labs( x = "Country", y = "Number of observations", fill = "Year", title = "20 most represented countries" ) + theme_gtree() + theme(legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm")) + guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 2))
```

We see on this graph that the observations across the different countries were collected during a period of 10 years and that a slight increase in the number of yearly observations has been seen in the last years, from 2022 to 2024.

# Source and Platform Bias

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
*— Nataliia*
:::

## Source Classification

Each observation's source field is matched against keyword rules to produce one of seven groups (ordered from most to least specific):

- **iNaturalist** — the largest citizen-science biodiversity platform worldwide.
- **Pl\@ntNet** — a plant-identification app with a stronger presence in French-speaking countries and the Global South.
- **Other citizen-science apps** — regional portals (e.g., Artportalen, iRecord, Naturgucker, NatureMapr).
- **GBIF (aggregator)** — re-distributes records from thousands of organisations; may *overlap* with any other group.
- **Institutional & survey data** — herbarium/museum collections and systematic field campaigns.
- **Reference & thematic databases** — compiled floristic atlases, global plant databases (e.g., BIEN, RAINBIO, Tropicos), Wikidata, and invasive-species tracking.
- **Other / unknown** — everything that did not match any keyword rule.

The keyword rules work well for English-language names and major platforms but can misclassify multilingual or opaque source names; the "Other / unknown" group likely includes recognisable sources whose names did not match any rule.

### Classification coverage

```{r classification-coverage}
coverage_stats <- df |>
  summarise(
    total        = n(),
    n_other      = sum(source_group == "Other / unknown"),
    n_classified = total - n_other,
    coverage     = n_classified / total,
    other_rate   = n_other / total
  )
```

Of all `r format_number(coverage_stats$total)` observations, **`r format_percent(coverage_stats$coverage)`** are assigned to one of the six named groups, and **`r format_percent(coverage_stats$other_rate)`** fall into "Other / unknown". The higher the coverage rate, the more reliably the source-group comparisons throughout this report represent the full dataset.

## Source Concentration

```{r source-concentration-data}
# Count by individual source name — for the Pareto and top-sources charts
source_counts <- df |>
  filter(source_group != "Other / unknown") |>
  count(source_raw, sort = TRUE, name = "observations") |>
  mutate(
    share            = observations / sum(observations),
    cumulative_share = cumsum(share),
    source_rank      = row_number()
  )

# Count by source group — reused throughout the report
source_group_counts <- df |>
  count(source_group, name = "observations") |>
  mutate(share = observations / sum(observations))

# Top source groups by total volume — used in later sections as well
top_source_groups <- source_group_counts |>
  arrange(desc(observations)) |>
  slice_head(n = top_n_sources) |>
  pull(source_group) |>
  as.character()

inat_share    <- source_group_counts$share[source_group_counts$source_group == "iNaturalist"]
citizen_share <- sum(source_group_counts$share[
  source_group_counts$source_group %in%
    c("iNaturalist", "Pl@ntNet", "Other citizen-science apps")
])
```

iNaturalist alone contributes **`r format_percent(inat_share)`** of all observations; the three citizen-science groups together account for **`r format_percent(citizen_share)`**.

```{r source-pareto, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(source_counts |> slice_head(n = 50), aes(x = source_rank)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = share), fill = "#2171B5", alpha = 0.75, width = 0.85) +
  geom_line(aes(y = cumulative_share), color = "#C23B22", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 25, 50)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title    = "A small number of sources explain most observations",
    subtitle = "Bars show individual source share; the red line shows cumulative share.\n\"Other / unknown\" excluded so the distribution of classifiable sources is visible.",
    x = "Source rank", y = "Share of classified observations"
  ) +
  theme_gtree()
```

The Pareto chart shows extreme source concentration: a handful of individual sources account for the vast majority of classified observations, and the cumulative share curve flattens quickly. This means that any systematic bias in the top few sources will propagate through the entire dataset.

```{r source-group-bar, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(source_group_counts,
       aes(x = reorder(source_group, observations), y = observations, fill = source_group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = format_percent(share)), hjust = -0.08, size = 3.2) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = source_colors) +
  labs(
    title    = "Observation share by source group",
    subtitle = "Citizen-science platforms dominate. GBIF (aggregator) is shown separately.",
    x = NULL, y = "Observations"
  ) +
  theme_gtree()
```

The bar chart confirms that citizen-science platforms collectively dominate the dataset, with iNaturalist as the single largest contributor. Institutional and reference sources, while individually smaller, cover regions and taxa that citizen-science platforms may miss.

## What Is in "Other / Unknown"?

```{r other-source-data}
other_source_top <- df |>
  filter(source_group == "Other / unknown") |>
  count(source_raw, sort = TRUE, name = "observations") |>
  mutate(share_of_other = observations / sum(observations)) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)

n_other_sources <- n_distinct(df$source_raw[df$source_group == "Other / unknown"])
```

"Other / unknown" contains `r format_number(n_other_sources)` individually named sources that did not match any keyword rule. The chart below shows the largest contributors within this heterogeneous catch-all group.

```{r other-source-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3}
ggplot(other_source_top,
       aes(x = reorder(str_trunc(source_raw, 45), observations), y = observations)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2171B5", width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = format_percent(share_of_other)), hjust = -0.08, size = 3.1) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.16))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Largest individual sources inside \"Other / unknown\"",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "\"Other / unknown\" contains ", format_number(n_other_sources),
      " differently-named sources in total."
    ),
    x = NULL, y = "Observations",
    caption  = "Percentages are share of the Other / unknown group, not of the whole dataset."
  ) +
  theme_gtree()
```

## Countries and Regional Coverage

```{r country-source-data}
top_country_values <- df |>
  count(country_code, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = top_n_countries) |>
  pull(country_code)

country_source <- df |>
  filter(country_code %in% top_country_values) |>
  mutate(source_group_plot = ifelse(
    as.character(source_group) %in% top_source_groups,
    as.character(source_group), "Other / unknown"
  )) |>
  count(country_code, source_group_plot, name = "observations") |>
  group_by(country_code) |>
  mutate(country_total = sum(observations), share = observations / country_total) |>
  ungroup()

country_order <- country_source |>
  distinct(country_code, country_total) |>
  arrange(country_total) |>
  pull(country_code)

country_source <- country_source |>
  mutate(
    country_code     = factor(country_code, levels = country_order),
    source_group_plot = factor(source_group_plot, levels = source_group_levels)
  )
```

```{r country-source-stacked-share, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4}
ggplot(country_source, aes(x = country_code, y = share, fill = source_group_plot)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = source_colors, drop = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Source composition differs by country",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Top ", top_n_countries,
      " countries by observations; bars sum to 100% within each country.\n",
      "GBIF (aggregator) is shown separately — its true source mix is unknown."
    ),
    x = NULL, y = "Share of country observations", fill = "Source group"
  ) +
  theme_gtree()
```

The stacked bar chart reveals that source composition varies sharply by country. Some countries are almost entirely supplied by a single platform (e.g. iNaturalist in the US), while others draw from a more balanced mix. Countries dominated by a single source inherit that platform's geographic and taxonomic biases.

Shannon entropy converted to "effective number of source groups" quantifies source diversity per country (1 = one source dominates).

```{r country-diversity-data}
# Shannon entropy -> "effective number of source groups" per country.
shannon_diversity <- function(counts) {
  p <- counts / sum(counts)
  p <- p[p > 0]
  -sum(p * log(p))
}

country_diversity <- df |>
  count(country_code, source_group, name = "observations") |>
  group_by(country_code) |>
  summarise(
    total_observations = sum(observations),
    effective_sources  = exp(shannon_diversity(observations)),
    dominant_source    = as.character(source_group[which.max(observations)]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_observations)) |>
  slice_head(n = top_n_countries) |>
  mutate(country_code = factor(country_code, levels = rev(country_code)))
```

```{r source-diversity-country, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4}
ggplot(country_diversity, aes(x = country_code, y = effective_sources, fill = dominant_source)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = source_colors, drop = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title    = "How source-diverse are the largest country samples?",
    subtitle = "Effective number of source groups is low when one source dominates a country.",
    x = NULL, y = "Effective number of source groups", fill = "Dominant source"
  ) +
  theme_gtree()
```

Countries with low effective source diversity (close to 1) are essentially single-source samples, meaning their apparent species composition and geographic coverage are shaped almost entirely by one platform's user base. Countries with higher diversity draw from multiple independent collection efforts, making their data more robust to any single platform's biases.

## Sources and Taxonomic Groups

```{r taxonomic-source-data}
df <- df |> mutate(family_clean = ifelse(level1_family == "" | is.na(level1_family), "Unknown family", level1_family))

top_families <- df |>
  count(family_clean, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = top_n_taxa) |>
  pull(family_clean)

family_source <- df |>
  filter(family_clean %in% top_families) |>
  mutate(source_group_plot = ifelse(
    as.character(source_group) %in% top_source_groups,
    as.character(source_group), "Other / unknown"
  )) |>
  count(family_clean, source_group_plot, name = "observations") |>
  group_by(family_clean) |>
  mutate(share = observations / sum(observations)) |>
  ungroup()

family_order <- family_source |>
  group_by(family_clean) |>
  summarise(total = sum(observations)) |>
  arrange(total) |>
  pull(family_clean)

family_source <- family_source |>
  mutate(
    family_clean      = factor(family_clean, levels = family_order),
    source_group_plot = factor(source_group_plot, levels = source_group_levels)
  )
```

```{r taxon-source-share, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4}
ggplot(family_source, aes(x = family_clean, y = share, fill = source_group_plot)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = source_colors, drop = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Source composition by plant family",
    subtitle = "Bars sum to 100% within each taxonomic group.",
    x = NULL, y = "Share of observations", fill = "Source group"
  ) +
  theme_gtree()
```

The source mix is not uniform across plant families. Some families are predominantly recorded through citizen-science apps, while others rely more heavily on institutional surveys or reference databases. Families that are primarily recorded by a single source type may have geographic or temporal gaps that mirror that source's coverage limitations.

## Geographic Footprints of Data Sources

```{r source-map-data}
#| cache: true
map_source_groups <- source_group_counts |>
  filter(!source_group %in% c("Other / unknown")) |>
  arrange(desc(observations)) |>
  slice_head(n = top_n_source_maps) |>
  pull(source_group) |>
  as.character()

map_data_by_source <- df |>
  filter(as.character(source_group) %in% map_source_groups,
         !is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude),
         between(latitude, -90, 90), between(longitude, -180, 180)) |>
  group_by(source_group) |>
  group_modify(~ sample_up_to(.x, source_map_sample_n)) |>
  ungroup()

world_outline <- ggplot2::map_data("world")
world_outline_plot <- world_outline |>
  filter(region != "Antarctica")
```

```{r source-faceted-map, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = world_outline_plot, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "gray96", color = "gray82", linewidth = 0.12, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = map_data_by_source, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude),
             alpha = 0.12, size = 0.22, color = "#1F5B74") +
  facet_wrap(~ source_group, ncol = 2) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-180, 180), ylim = c(-60, 85), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Geographic coverage of major source groups",
    subtitle = "Different source groups leave visibly different spatial footprints.",
    x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude",
    caption  = "Points show recording locations, not species ranges. Points are sampled for readability."
  ) +
  theme_map_gtree()
```

The faceted map reveals strikingly different spatial footprints across source groups. iNaturalist provides the most geographically widespread coverage but is concentrated in North America, Europe, and Oceania. Pl\@ntNet complements it with stronger presence in French-speaking Africa and parts of South America. Institutional and survey sources tend to fill in localised regions that citizen-science platforms miss. These differences mean that where the dataset is geographically strong or weak depends directly on which sources are active in a given region.

# Temporal Development

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
*— Nataliia*
:::

## Observation Volume Over Time

```{r yearly-counts}
yearly_counts <- df |>
  filter(year >= start_year, year <= end_year) |>
  count(year, name = "observations") |>
  right_join(tibble(year = start_year:end_year), by = "year") |>
  mutate(observations    = ifelse(is.na(observations), 0L, observations)) |>
  arrange(year) |>
  mutate(absolute_change = observations - lag(observations))

growth_summary    <- yearly_counts |> filter(!is.na(absolute_change))
strongest_growth  <- growth_summary |> slice_max(absolute_change, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
strongest_decline <- growth_summary |> slice_min(absolute_change, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

first_year_count <- yearly_counts$observations[yearly_counts$year == start_year]
last_year_count  <- yearly_counts$observations[yearly_counts$year == end_year]
overall_change   <- (last_year_count - first_year_count) / first_year_count
```

Between `r start_year` and `r end_year`, observations changed from **`r format_number(first_year_count)`** to **`r format_number(last_year_count)`**, an overall change of **`r format_percent(overall_change)`**.

```{r line-observations-by-year, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(yearly_counts, aes(x = year, y = observations)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2171B5", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(color = "#2171B5", size = 2.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = start_year:end_year) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Number of tree observations by year", x = "Year", y = "Observations") +
  theme_gtree()
```

```{r yearly-growth-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(growth_summary, aes(x = year, y = absolute_change, fill = absolute_change >= 0)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray35", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = format_number(absolute_change)),
    vjust = ifelse(growth_summary$absolute_change >= 0, -0.35, 1.15),
    size  = 3.1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = start_year:end_year) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.12, 0.16))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#2171B5", "FALSE" = "#C23B22")) +
  labs(
    title   = "Year-to-year change in observations",
    x = "Year", y = "Change in observations",
    caption = paste0("Year-to-year changes are calculated within the ", start_year, "–", end_year, " dataset period.")
  ) +
  theme_gtree()
```

The strongest growth occurs in **`r strongest_growth$year`** (+`r format_number(strongest_growth$absolute_change)` observations), and the strongest decline in **`r strongest_decline$year`** (`r format_number(strongest_decline$absolute_change)`).

## Which Sources Drive the Temporal Trend?

```{r source-year-data}
# Observations per year and source group
source_year <- df |>
  filter(year >= start_year, year <= end_year) |>
  mutate(source_group_plot = ifelse(
    as.character(source_group) %in% top_source_groups,
    as.character(source_group), "Other / unknown"
  )) |>
  count(year, source_group_plot, name = "observations") |>
  right_join(
    expand.grid(year = start_year:end_year,
                source_group_plot = source_group_levels),
    by = c("year", "source_group_plot")
  ) |>
  mutate(observations = ifelse(is.na(observations), 0L, observations)) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(
    share = observations / sum(observations),
    share = ifelse(is.nan(share), 0, share)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(source_group_plot = factor(source_group_plot, levels = source_group_levels))
```

```{r stacked-area-source-year, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(source_year, aes(x = year, y = observations, fill = source_group_plot)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.9, linewidth = 0.15, color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = start_year:end_year) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = source_colors, drop = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Observation volume by source group and year",
    subtitle = "A rising source group can drive the apparent growth of the full dataset.",
    x = "Year", y = "Observations", fill = "Source group"
  ) +
  theme_gtree()
```

The stacked area chart shows that the dataset's overall growth is largely driven by the expansion of citizen-science platforms, particularly iNaturalist. When iNaturalist's contribution grows, the total observation count rises accordingly, meaning the overall trend reflects platform adoption more than any change in tree populations.

```{r source-share-year, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(source_year, aes(x = year, y = share, fill = source_group_plot)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = start_year:end_year) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = source_colors, drop = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Source composition by year",
    subtitle = "Bars sum to 100% within each year.",
    x = "Year", y = "Share of observations", fill = "Source group",
    caption  = paste0("Shares are calculated within each year of the ", start_year, "–", end_year, " dataset period.")
  ) +
  theme_gtree()
```

The year-by-year source share view shows whether the source mix is shifting over time. If one source group's share is growing while others shrink, the dataset's overall character is changing — even if total volume increases. A stable composition would suggest that all sources are growing at roughly the same rate.

```{r source-growth-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
largest_source_growth <- source_year |>
  arrange(source_group_plot, year) |>
  group_by(source_group_plot) |>
  mutate(source_change = observations - lag(observations)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(!is.na(source_change)) |>
  slice_max(source_change, n = 8, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(label = paste0(year, ": ", source_group_plot))

ggplot(largest_source_growth,
       aes(x = reorder(label, source_change), y = source_change, fill = source_group_plot)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = source_colors, drop = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Largest source-specific yearly increases", x = NULL, y = "Increase from previous year") +
  theme_gtree()
```

The chart above highlights the single largest year-over-year jumps for each source group, making it easy to identify which platforms drove the biggest surges in data volume and when those surges occurred.

## Geographic Coverage Over Time

This subsection examines whether the dataset's geographic reach has expanded over time by looking at the rate of new countries entering the dataset and by comparing observation locations at selected snapshot years.

```{r country-coverage-data}
country_year <- df |>
  filter(year >= start_year, year <= end_year) |>
  count(year, country_code, name = "observations")

country_first_year <- country_year |>
  group_by(country_code) |>
  summarise(first_observed_year = min(year), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r new-countries-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.2}
new_countries <- country_first_year |>
  filter(first_observed_year > start_year) |>
  count(first_observed_year, name = "new_countries") |>
  right_join(tibble(first_observed_year = (start_year + 1):end_year), by = "first_observed_year") |>
  mutate(new_countries = ifelse(is.na(new_countries), 0L, new_countries))

countries_at_start <- sum(country_first_year$first_observed_year == start_year)

ggplot(new_countries, aes(x = first_observed_year, y = new_countries)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2171B5", width = 0.72) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = (start_year + 1):end_year) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title   = "New countries entering the dataset by year",
    x = "First observed year in period", y = "New countries",
    caption = paste0(
      start_year, " is excluded: ", countries_at_start,
      " countries already had observations in the first year of the window."
    )
  ) +
  theme_gtree()
```

The rate of new countries entering the dataset shows whether the geographic reach is still expanding. A declining rate suggests that most accessible countries are already covered and further growth is primarily a matter of densification rather than discovery of new regions.

The maps below show observation locations at four snapshot years, revealing whether records spread into new regions or simply become denser in existing ones.

```{r map-snapshots-data}
#| cache: true
snapshot_years_valid <- snapshot_years[snapshot_years >= start_year & snapshot_years <= end_year]

map_data_by_year <- df |>
  filter(year %in% snapshot_years_valid,
         !is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude),
         between(latitude, -90, 90), between(longitude, -180, 180)) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  group_modify(~ sample_up_to(.x, world_map_sample_n)) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r map-snapshots-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = world_outline_plot, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "gray96", color = "gray82", linewidth = 0.12, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = map_data_by_year, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude),
             alpha = 0.15, size = 0.22, color = "#1F5B74") +
  facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 2) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-180, 180), ylim = c(-60, 85), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Map snapshots of observations over time",
    subtitle = "Selected years show whether records spread or intensify in existing regions.",
    x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude",
    caption  = "Points are sampled per year for readability."
  ) +
  theme_map_gtree()
```

Comparing the four snapshot years shows that the geographic footprint of the dataset was already broadly established early in the period: North America, Europe, and parts of Oceania and South America are visible from the first panel. Later panels show a clear increase in point density within these same regions, but comparatively little expansion into previously unsampled areas such as central Africa, interior Asia, or the Amazon basin. This confirms that the dataset's growth over time has been primarily a matter of intensification rather than geographic expansion.

# Taxonomic Composition and Geographic Patterns

## Species observed in this dataset

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
*— Anna*
:::

What are the different tree families referenced in this dataset?

```{r level0-count-plot}
#| cache: true
#| fig-height: 3.5
level0_count <- data %>% count(level0, sort = TRUE)

ggplot(level0_count, aes(x = reorder(level0, n), y = n)) + geom_col(fill = "steelblue") + coord_flip() + labs( x = "Plant category", y = "Number of observations", title = "Number of observations for each plant category" ) + theme_gtree()
```

Definition of each tree category:

-   Evergreen Needleleaf: An evergreen needleleaf refers to woody vegetation that retains needle-like or scale-like foliage year-round

-   Evergreen Broadleaf: An evergreen broadleaf is a plant or tree that has wide, flat leaves (rather than needles or scales) and retains its foliage year-round

-   Deciduous Broadleaf: a diverse group of flowering plants (angiosperms) characterized by flat leaves that are shed annually before winter (Oak, Maple, Beech, Birch, and Poplar/Aspen)

-   Deciduous Needleleaf : a unique group of conifers that, unlike their evergreen counterparts, shed all their needles annually in the autumn (rare trees)

We see here that a very important part of the observations in this dataset are deciduous broadleaf trees. It makes sense because most of the tree species spread across the world are part of this family. On the contrary, Deciduous needleleaf are rare and located in much more restricted areas.

What are the different taxonomic families represented in this dataset and in which proportion are they represented?

```{r family-count-plot}
#| cache: true
# Number of level1_categories
level1_count <- data %>% count(level1_family, sort=TRUE) 

# selection of the 20 most represented families

top20 <- level1_count %>% slice_head(n = 20)

ggplot(top20, aes(x = reorder(level1_family, n), y = n)) + geom_col(fill = "steelblue") + labs( x = "Taxonomic family", y = "Number of observations", title = "Top 20 taxonomic families by number of observations" ) + theme_gtree() + theme( axis.text.x = element_text( angle = 45, hjust = 1 ) )
```

Again, here we see that the most represented taxonomic families in this dataset are also the most represented ones across the world, especially in North America, Europe and the north of Asia, where most of the data come from. However, as the source bias analysis above shows, this apparent representativeness should be interpreted with caution: the dataset reflects where observers and platforms are most active, not a systematic global survey.

## Geographical distribution of the observations

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
*— Anna*
:::

How are the trees distributed depending on the latitude?

```{r latitude-distribution-plots}
#| cache: true
ggplot(data, aes(x = latitude)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "forestgreen", color = "white") + scale_x_reverse() + labs( title = "Distribution of the observations depending on the latitude", x = "Latitude (°)", y = "Number of observations" ) + annotate( "text", x = min(data$latitude, na.rm = TRUE),
    y = -Inf,
    label = "South",
    vjust = 1,
    hjust = 0,
    col="darkgreen"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = max(data$latitude, na.rm = TRUE), y = -Inf, label = "North", vjust = 1, hjust = 1, col="darkgreen" ) + theme_gtree() + coord_cartesian(clip = "off") + theme( plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 30, 10) )

# density curve

ggplot(data, aes(x = latitude)) + geom_density(fill = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.5) + labs( title = "Tree density depending on the latitude", x = "Latitude (°)", y = "Density" ) + theme_gtree() + annotate( "text", x = min(data$latitude, na.rm = TRUE),
    y = -Inf,
    label = "South",
    vjust = 2,
    hjust = 0,
    col="darkgreen"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = max(data$latitude, na.rm = TRUE), y = -Inf, label = "North", vjust = 2, hjust = 1, col="darkgreen" ) + coord_cartesian(clip = "off") + theme( plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 30, 10) )
```

We see on this graph that the observation density is much more important on the north hemisphere than in the south hemisphere, but this can be linked to the amount of land that differs between north and south hemisphere or the difference in the amount of observations between the two hemispheres.

Larger representations are also often used in ecological studies, because 5° latitudinal bands contain a satisfying amount of information without showing too much noise.

```{r latitude-band-count}
#| cache: true
lat_band <- data %>% mutate(lat_bin = floor(latitude / 5) * 5) %>% count(lat_bin)

ggplot(lat_band, aes(x = lat_bin, y = n)) + geom_col(fill = "steelblue") + labs( title = "Number of trees for each band of 5° latitude", x = "Latitude", y = "Number of observations" ) + theme_gtree() 
```

The same conclusions can be drawn as before.

We usually take 5° slices because it is small enough to find local tendencies but also big enough to avoid noise and too much non useful information and generally fine enough to reveal geographical patterns (climatic gradients, biodiversity, species distribution, etc.) without creating too much noise.

## Geographical observations of species

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
*— Anna*
:::

How does the latitude influences the different species observed? (Lattitude and specific richness)

```{r global-species-richness-latitude}
#| cache: true
richness <- data %>% mutate(lat_bin = floor(latitude / 5) * 5) %>% group_by(lat_bin) %>% summarise(species_richness = n_distinct(species_key))

ggplot(richness, aes(lat_bin, species_richness)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() + labs( title = "Specific richness depending on the latitude", x = "Latitude", y = "Number of species (Specific richness)" ) + theme_gtree()+ scale_x_reverse()
```

Species richness: simple count of the number of different species present in a specific biological community, landscape, or region Much more important in the north hemisphere than in the south hemisphere more important in temperate areas, much lower at the equator and near the poles.

We see here that the maximum species richness are very close in the two hemisphere, but that the distribution is broader in the northern hemisphere than in the southern hemisphere (it is also because trees grow at higher latitudes in the northern hemisphere than in the southern hemisphere). Similar environmental conditions can be found in the two hemispheres but they are not spread following the same pattern.

How does the longitude influences the diffrent species observed (longitude and specifi richness)?

```{r global-species-richness-longitude}
#| cache: true
richness_long <- data %>% mutate(long_bin = floor(longitude / 5) * 5) %>% group_by(long_bin) %>% summarise(species_richness = n_distinct(species_key))

ggplot(richness_long, aes(long_bin, species_richness)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() + labs( title = "Species richness by longitude", x = "Longitude", y = "Number of species observed" ) + theme_gtree()+ scale_x_reverse()
```

We see here that areas with a lot of specific richness correspond to the continental areas, but not much more can be taken out of this graph.

What is the local specific richness across the world?

```{r global-richness-grid-map}
#| cache: true
richness_grid <- data %>% 
  mutate( lat_bin = floor(latitude / 1) * 1, long_bin = floor(longitude / 1) * 1 ) %>% group_by(lat_bin, long_bin) %>% summarise( richness = n_distinct(species_key), .groups = "drop" )

world <- if (exists("world_outline_plot")) {
  world_outline_plot
} else {
  ggplot2::map_data("world") |>
    filter(region != "Antarctica")
}

ggplot() + geom_tile( data = richness_grid, aes( x = long_bin + 2.5, y = lat_bin + 2.5, fill = richness ) ) + geom_polygon( data = world, aes(long, lat, group = group), fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.2 ) + scale_fill_gradientn( colours = c( "yellow", "orange", "darkred" ), name = "Species richness" ) + coord_fixed(1.3) + labs( title = "Global tree species richness", x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude" ) + theme_gtree()
```

We see here that, in the areas presenting observations, the species richness does not present too important variations and is homogenous in most areas. By crossing this with the previous results, we can think that the species richness does not vary but that the species involved do vary across the world.

How are the different tree species distributed depending on the latitude? Here, we only check for the most represented species.

```{r top-species-latitude}
#| cache: true
# latitude distribution of the 20 most frequent species
top_species <- data %>% count(level3_species, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = 20)

lat_species <- data %>% filter(level3_species %in% top_species$level3_species) %>% mutate(lat_bin = floor(latitude)) %>% count(level3_species, lat_bin)

ggplot(lat_species, aes(lat_bin, n)) + geom_line() + facet_wrap(~level3_species)
```

With this figure, we see that among the most represented species in this dataset, they present different world distributions. Most of them are mostly present in the northern hemisphere, but some are also present in the southern hemisphere (such as Dombeya acrifolia), and some are almost evenly present in the two hemispheres, such as Cornus acuminata.

Another representation could be a heatmap representing the species depenting on the latitude:

```{r top-species-latitude-heatmap}
#| cache: true
top50 <- data %>% count(level3_species, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = 50)

heat <- data %>% filter(level3_species %in% top50$level3_species) %>% mutate(lat_bin = floor(latitude)) %>% count(level3_species, lat_bin)

ggplot(heat, aes(lat_bin, reorder(level3_species, n), fill = n)) + geom_tile()
```

Again, we see here that most species are present mostly in the northern hemisphere, but some can also be present in both hemisphere or only in the southern hemisphere or near the equator (Guazuma umifolia, a tree largely present in Latin America and really rare in other areas).

boxplot family x latitude

```{r family-latitude-boxplot}
#| cache: true
top20_family <- data %>% count(level1_family, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = 20)

ggplot( data %>% filter(level1_family %in% top20_family$level1_family), aes(x = reorder(level1_family, latitude, median), y = latitude) ) + geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") + coord_flip()
```

Same but on a map. Both maps below use the shared worldwide point-map subsample (see Methodology for subsampling details).

```{r family-map-samples}
#| cache: true
data_sample <- df_world_map_sample

ggplot(data_sample, aes(longitude, latitude)) +
  geom_polygon(data = world, aes(long, lat, group = group), fill = "lightgrey", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.03, size = 0.05) +
  coord_fixed() + theme_gtree()

# one map for each family (20 first families)
top_families <- data %>% count(level1_family, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = 12) %>% pull(level1_family)

data_top <- df_world_map_base %>%
  filter(level1_family %in% top_families) %>%
  group_by(level1_family) %>%
  group_modify(~ sample_up_to(.x, world_map_sample_n)) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(data_top, aes(longitude, latitude)) +
  geom_polygon(data = world, aes(long, lat, group = group), fill = "lightgrey", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.03, size = 0.05) +
  facet_wrap(~ level1_family) + coord_fixed() + theme_gtree() +
  labs( title = "Spatial distribution of the 12 most abundant families" )
```

On this visualization, we can see the distribution of the different taxonomical families across the world: - families are very widely spread across the world such as the Asteraceae: this family contains a very large amount of different species, that live in temperate areas. They can survive various non-extreme conditions. - families are observed in more restrictive areas, such as the families Ericaceae and Pinaceae: these families are very adapted to cold and unwelcoming places such as the tundra and boreal forests or places that are at a high altitude.

# Worldwide Distribution of the Data

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
*— Camille*
:::

How are observations distributed globally, and what does this reveal about sampling bias and taxonomic diversity? This section addresses four guiding questions:

1.  Where are observations geographically concentrated, and does the coverage reflect ecological reality or observer activity?
2.  How does the distribution of foliage types vary across latitudes and continents?
3.  How does taxonomic richness compare across continents once differences in sampling effort are accounted for?
4.  Has the spatial coverage of the dataset expanded or merely intensified over the years?

In this section, the aim is to understand how observations are distributed globally, both spatially and temporally. This distribution matters because it directly shapes how the rest of the dataset should be interpreted: an over-representation of certain regions may reflect sampling bias (the activity of contributors in the field) rather than the true state of global tree biodiversity. It is therefore essential to characterize where and when the data was collected, and to identify areas of high and low sampling density. We start by examining the overall geographical spread of observations across continents, before looking more closely at how taxonomic diversity (families, genus, species) is distributed in space. Finally, we analyze how sampling effort has evolved over time, both globally and by continent, to assess whether spatial biases have shifted across the years.

## Pre-Processing

For this analysis, observations are grouped by continent rather than by country. With data spanning more than 210 countries, a country-level analysis would fragment the dataset into categories too small and numerous to reveal meaningful patterns, while a continent-level grouping provides a small number of interpretable regions, each large enough to support robust comparisons of taxonomic diversity and temporal trends. The continent for each observation was derived by spatially joining the point coordinates (longitude, latitude) with a world countries shapefile (rnaturalearth). This approach, however, relies on administrative continent boundaries, which do not always align with the geographical logic relevant to this study. Two adjustments were therefore necessary:

-   Russia is administratively classified as a single entity, but spans two geographical continents. Observations were reassigned to Europe or Asia based on the conventional Ural Mountains boundary (60°E longitude).
-   Réunion Island, despite being a French overseas territory, is geographically located in the Indian Ocean off the African coast, and was therefore reassigned to Africa rather than being grouped with other European territories.

Observations for which no continent could be determined, as well as those located over open ocean (e.g., isolated island territories not covered by the country shapefile), were excluded from the dataset.

The resulting dataset, with the added continent column, is previewed in @tbl-dataset.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dataset
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| tbl-cap: "An overview of the first few rows of the dataset"
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| tbl-height: 3

df_preview <- head(df) |>
  select(sample_id, country_code, level0, level1_family, level2_genus,
         level3_species, source, year, continent)
if (params$latex) {
  kableExtra::kbl(df_preview, booktabs = TRUE, longtable = FALSE) |>
    kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("scale_down", "hold_position"))
} else {
  kable(df_preview)
}
```

To ensure visual consistency throughout this section, each continent is assigned a fixed color, shown in @fig-couleur-continent. This color scheme is derived from the Okabe-Ito palette, chosen for its colorblind-friendly properties, and is applied consistently across all subsequent maps and charts to facilitate comparison between figures.

```{r}
#| label: fig-couleur-continent
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Colour scheme used to represent the continents in the following figures"
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-height: 1.8
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-align: center


continent_colors <- c(
  "Africa"        = "#E69F00",  # orange
  "Asia"          = "#D55E00",  # red-orange
  "Europe"        = "#0072B2",  # blue
  "North America" = "#009E73",  # green
  "South America" = "#56B4E9",  # light blue
  "Oceania"       = "#CC79A7"   # purple
)


ggplot(
  data.frame(
    continent = names(continent_colors),
    color = continent_colors
  ),
  aes(x = continent, y = 1, fill = continent)
) +

  geom_tile(width = 0.95, height = 0.8) +

  scale_fill_manual(values = continent_colors) +

  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(continent, "\n", color)),
    size = 3.2, vjust = 0.5
  ) +

  theme_void() +

  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

## Global overview

This first subsection provides a global overview of where observations are located. The goal is twofold: first, to visualize the overall spatial coverage of the dataset and assess which regions of the world are represented; second, to quantify this coverage at the continent level in order to detect potential imbalances in sampling effort. @fig-map-continent projects a reproducible subsample of observations on a world map, colored by continent, offering a first visual impression of the dataset's geographical spread without plotting millions of individual points. @fig-bar-continent then complements this map with a quantitative summary, showing the total number of observations recorded per continent. Finally, @fig-density-map goes one step further by highlighting areas of high and low observation density within continents, revealing local concentrations that a simple point map or continent-level count cannot capture on their own. For instance, distinguishing a continent with many observations spread evenly across its territory from one where the same volume of observations is concentrated in a few localized hotspots.

```{r}
#| label: fig-map-continent
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Geographical projection of observations by continent"
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-align: center


world_map <- if (exists("world_outline_plot")) {
  world_outline_plot
} else {
  map_data("world") |>
    filter(region != "Antarctica")
}


 ggplot() +
   
  geom_polygon(data = world_map,
               aes(long, lat, group = group),
               fill = "grey92", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
   
  geom_point(data = df_world_map_sample,
             aes(longitude, latitude, colour = continent),
             alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
   
  scale_color_manual(values = continent_colors, guide = "none") +
   
  coord_fixed(1.3, xlim = c(-180, 180), ylim = c(-60, 85)) +
   
  labs(caption = paste("Displayed points:", format_number(nrow(df_world_map_sample)), "of", format_number(nrow(df_world_map_base)), "valid mapped observations.")) +
   
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

```

@fig-map-continent shows a strongly uneven geographical coverage of observations. North America (green) and Europe (blue) display a dense, near-continuous coverage, closely following major population centers and road networks (a pattern typical of citizen science platforms like iNaturalist, where sampling effort is driven by observer density rather than tree distribution alone). Asia (orange) covers a considerable geographical extent, but coverage is markedly uneven: it is dense in East Asia, India, and along the Trans-Siberian corridor, yet visibly sparse across Central Asia and Siberia's interior. Africa (yellow) shows a similar contrast, with observations concentrated in South Africa, East Africa, and coastal West Africa, while the Congo Basin and the Sahara remain largely unsampled. South America (light blue) is dominated by coastal Brazil and the Andean corridor, with the Amazon interior almost entirely absent from the dataset despite hosting one of the highest levels of tree biodiversity on Earth. Oceania (pink) is essentially limited to Australia's populated coastline and a scattering of Pacific islands. Overall, this map already suggests that observation density mirrors human accessibility and citizen-science activity more closely than it reflects actual tree biodiversity (a hypothesis further examined in the following density map @fig-density-map).

```{r}
#| label: fig-bar-continent
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Total number of observations by continent"
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-height: 5


df_n_obs <- df %>%
  count(continent, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = n / sum(n),
    label = scales::percent(percentage, accuracy = 0.1)
  )


ggplot(df_n_obs, aes(x = reorder(continent, n), y = n)) +
  
  geom_col(aes(fill = continent)) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(values = continent_colors) +
  
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label),
    hjust = -0.1
  ) +
  
  expand_limits(y = max(df_n_obs$n) * 1.05) +
  
  coord_flip() +
  
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Nb. obs."
  ) +
  
  theme_gtree() +
  
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

@fig-bar-continent quantifies the imbalance already suggested by @fig-map-continent. North America and Europe together account for 74.4% of all observations (41.3% and 33.1% respectively), despite representing only a fraction of the world's land area and tree biodiversity. Oceania follows at 10.3%, largely driven by Australia, before a sharp drop to South America (6.6%), Asia (5.5%) and Africa (3.3%). This ranking reveals an important nuance compared to the previous map. Although Asia appeared visually extensive in @fig-map-continent (spanning a wide longitudinal range with a dense cluster of points), it accounts for only 5.5% of total observations, far below Europe or North America. This apparent contradiction is simply a matter of scale: individual points can appear numerous and spread out on a map while still representing a small share of a dataset containing several million observations overall. This illustrates why the two figures are complementary. The map shows where observations are located, while the bar chart shows how much each region actually contributes to the dataset.

The density map below is computed on a reproducible random subsample (see Methodology for the subsampling rationale).

```{r}
#| label: fig-density-map
#| eval: true
#| cache: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Geographical density of observations"
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-width: 10

set.seed(map_sample_seed)
df_density <- df[is.finite(df$longitude) & is.finite(df$latitude), ]
df_density <- df_density[sample(nrow(df_density), min(density_map_sample_n, nrow(df_density))), ]

ggplot() +

  # Base map
  geom_polygon(
    data = world_map,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "grey90", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1
  ) +

  # 2D density
  geom_density_2d_filled(
    data = df_density,
    aes(x = longitude, y = latitude),
    contour_var = "ndensity",
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +

  scale_fill_viridis_d(
    option = "cividis",
    name = "Relative density"
  ) +
  
  coord_fixed(1.3, xlim = c(-180, 180), ylim = c(-60, 85)) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

```

*Note: the density estimate is based on a reproducible random subsample of 50,000 observations (drawn with the report-level map seed from the full dataset), rather than all 6.26 million records. Passing the full dataset to `geom_density_2d_filled()` caused a crash in ggplot2 3.5.2 due to memory limitations in the internal stat pipeline. At this sample size, kernel density estimation produces a visually identical result, as the smoothing operation is stable well below this threshold.*

@fig-density-map confirms and refines the pattern already observed in the previous two figures by revealing that observations are not only concentrated on certain continents, but highly clustered within a small number of localized hotspots. The most intense concentration is found in Western Europe (particularly around France, Germany and the United Kingdom), followed closely by the northeastern United States. Secondary hotspots appear along the U.S. West Coast, in Central America, in southeastern Australia, and around Taiwan / southern Japan, while the vast majority of the remaining land surface, including most of Africa, Asia and South America, shows minimal to no density. This concentration pattern reinforces the hypothesis raised earlier: sampling effort appears strongly correlated with population density and citizen-science activity rather than with the underlying distribution of tree biodiversity. Notably, even within high-observation continents such as North America (@fig-bar-continent), density is far from uniform. Most observations are concentrated along the East and West coasts, while large inland areas remain comparatively under-sampled.

Together, these three figures paint a consistent picture. The dataset's geographical coverage reflects observer accessibility and activity far more than actual global tree distribution, a limitation that should be kept in mind, particularly when interpreting taxonomic diversity by continent in the following sections.

## Spatial distribution of foliage types

Having established the overall geographical coverage of the dataset, this subsection shifts focus from where observations occur to what is being observed where. Each tree in the dataset is classified into one of four foliage types (Evergreen Broadleaf, Evergreen Needleleaf, Deciduous Broadleaf, or Deciduous Needleleaf). This classification closely tied to climate, since foliage strategy reflects how trees adapt to seasonal variation in temperature and water availability. The goal is therefore to examine whether these foliage types are distributed uniformly across the sampled regions, or whether they follow the climatic gradients expected from ecological theory, and to what extent this pattern can still be observed despite the sampling bias identified previously.

Three complementary perspectives are used to explore this question. @fig-maps-foliage first projects a reproducible subsample of observations for each foliage type, allowing their geographical range to be visualized directly on a world map. @fig-bar-foliage-continent then aggregates this information into a quantitative comparison, showing how foliage composition varies from one continent to another. Finally, @fig-ridge-latitude moves away from continental boundaries altogether, examining how the density of each foliage type is distributed along a continuous latitudinal gradient. This perspective is particularly relevant here, since climate (and therefore foliage strategy) is primarily structured by latitude rather than by administrative continental divisions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-maps-foliage
#| eval: true
#| cache: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Geographical distribution by type of foliage"
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-align: center


palette_level0 <- c(
  "Deciduous Broadleaf"  = "#E69F00",   
  "Evergreen Broadleaf"  = "#009E73",   
  "Evergreen Needleleaf" = "#0072B2",
  "Deciduous Needleleaf" = "#CC79A7"
)


ggplot() +
  
  geom_polygon(
    data = world_map,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "grey90", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  
  geom_point(
    data = df_world_map_sample_by_level0,
    aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, colour = level0),
    alpha = 0.35, size = 0.6
  ) +
  
  scale_colour_manual(values = palette_level0, guide = "none") +
  
  facet_wrap(~ level0, ncol = 2) +      # two categories per row
  
  coord_fixed(1.3, xlim = c(-180, 180), ylim = c(-60, 85)) +
  
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = paste("Displayed points: up to", format_number(world_map_sample_n), "per foliage type.")
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  
  theme(
    panel.grid  = element_blank(),
    strip.text  = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey94", colour = NA)
  )

```

@fig-maps-foliage reveals that Deciduous Broadleaf (orange) and Evergreen Broadleaf (green) share a broadly similar geographical footprint, both present across nearly all sampled continents and spanning a wide range of latitudes, from temperate to tropical regions. This similarity suggests that, at the continental scale visualized here, geographical presence alone does not clearly separate these two categories. A finer, latitude-based view is needed to detect any underlying climatic gradient between them, which is examined in @fig-ridge-latitude. Evergreen Needleleaf (blue) is most heavily concentrated across the boreal and temperate zones of the Northern Hemisphere (North America, Europe, and northern Asia) but is also present, at lower density, in the southern parts of South America, southern Africa, and Oceania, suggesting an association with temperate conditions more broadly rather than strictly cold northern climates. Deciduous Needleleaf (pink) remains overwhelmingly concentrated at high latitudes, primarily across Siberia and parts of Canada, with only a lower-density secondary presence in the United States and Europe, confirming that, unlike Evergreen Needleleaf, this foliage type stays largely confined to high-latitude regions overall.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bar-foliage-continent
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Geographical distribution by type of foliage"
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-align: center


df_level0 <- df %>%
  count(continent, level0, name = "n") %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100) %>%    # proportion for fair comparison across continents
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(continent = reorder(continent, n, sum))  # sort by total


ggplot(df_level0, aes(x = continent, y = pct, fill = level0)) +
  
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette_level0, name = "Foliage") +
  
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  
  coord_flip() +
  
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "Proportion of observations (%)"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

@fig-bar-foliage-continent complements the previous maps by quantifying, for each continent, the relative composition of foliage types, independent of each continent's overall sampling volume. A clear contrast emerges between temperate and tropical/subtropical continents. North America and Europe share a similar profile, dominated by Deciduous Broadleaf (around 60–70% of observations), followed by Evergreen Broadleaf as the second-largest category (roughly 25–30%), with Evergreen Needleleaf making up a smaller but still notable share (around 10%), a share not found at comparable levels on any other continent, consistent with the boreal/temperate conifer forests characteristic of these regions. Oceania and Africa, by contrast, are clearly dominated by Evergreen Broadleaf, which accounts for the majority of observations in both continents (over 75% in Oceania, around 60% in Africa), with Deciduous Broadleaf as a smaller secondary category. South America and Asia present an intermediate profile, with Evergreen Broadleaf and Deciduous Broadleaf nearly evenly split at close to 50% each, suggesting that these two continents span a broader mix of climatic zones, from tropical to temperate, rather than being dominated by a single climate regime. Across all four of these continents, Evergreen Needleleaf drops to a marginal share compared to North America and Europe, and Deciduous Needleleaf is nearly absent everywhere except for a very thin presence in North America, Europe, and Asia, consistent with the highly restricted geographical range already observed in @fig-maps-foliage. This continent-level breakdown reinforces the latitudinal pattern suggested by the maps: continents located predominantly at temperate latitudes (North America, Europe) show a foliage composition weighted toward deciduous and needleleaf strategies, while continents dominated by tropical or subtropical land area (Oceania, Africa) are dominated by evergreen broadleaf species, with South America and Asia sitting in between due to their wider climatic range. This distinction by continent, however, remains an approximation, since large countries such as the United States or China span multiple climatic zones. This limitation is directly addressed by @fig-ridge-latitude, which examines this relationship along a continuous latitudinal axis rather than through continental boundaries.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ridge-latitude
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of foliage types by latitude"
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-align: center


# Ridge plot
ggplot(df, aes(x = latitude, y = level0, fill = level0)) +
  
  # Climate reference lines (drawn before the curves so they appear underneath)
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0,    colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "solid") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 23.5, colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -23.5,colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 66.5, colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  
  # Density curves with transparency gradient (gradient under the curve)
  geom_density_ridges(
    aes(fill = level0),
    alpha       = 0.75,
    scale       = 1.8,         # overlap between curves (1 = no overlap)
    rel_min_height = 0.005,    # trims very low-density tails
    bandwidth   = 3,           # smoothing in degrees of latitude
    colour      = "white",
    linewidth   = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Climate zone annotations
  annotate("text", x = 0,     y = 0, label = "Equator",       angle = 90,
           vjust = 0, hjust=0, size = 3, colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = 23.5,  y = 0, label = "Tropic of Cancer", angle = 90,
           vjust = -0.4, hjust=0, size = 3, colour = "grey55") +
  annotate("text", x = -23.5, y = 0, label = "Tropic of Capricorn", angle = 90,
           vjust =  1.2, hjust=0, size = 3, colour = "grey55") +
  annotate("text", x = 66.5,  y = 0, label = "Arctic Circle", angle = 90,
           vjust = -0.4, hjust=0, size = 3, colour = "grey55") +
  
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette_level0, guide = "none") +
  
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(-60, 80, by = 10),
    labels = function(x) paste0(abs(x), ifelse(x >= 0, "°N", "°S")),
    limits = c(-60, 80)
  ) +
  
  labs(
    x        = "Latitude",
    y        = NULL
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y        = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.caption       = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey50", hjust = 0)
  )

```

@fig-ridge-latitude confirms and refines, with much greater precision, the patterns suggested by the previous map and bar chart. Evergreen Needleleaf (blue) shows the most clearly defined latitudinal signal in the entire figure: a sharp, dominant peak around 45–50°N, with only a small secondary bump around 30–40°S, confirming that this foliage type is overwhelmingly associated with Northern Hemisphere temperate/boreal latitudes, with a much smaller presence in the Southern Hemisphere's temperate zone. Deciduous Needleleaf (pink) is similarly concentrated at high northern latitudes, with a pronounced peak around 45–55°N and virtually no presence in the Southern Hemisphere. Its distribution is the narrowest and most latitude-restricted of the four foliage types, consistent with its very limited geographical range observed in @fig-maps-foliage. Deciduous Broadleaf (orange) is dominated by a large peak around 45–50°N, overlapping closely with the two needleleaf types, alongside a much smaller secondary bump near 10°N and a minor bump around 30°S. Evergreen Broadleaf (green) stands out as the most latitudinally spread category, with density visible almost continuously from 40°S to 50°N, including a distinct concentration in the tropical band (0–20°N) that is more pronounced than for the other three types, plus a bump around 30–40°S and a peak around 45–50°N that overlaps with Deciduous Broadleaf. This last point directly resolves the ambiguity raised in @fig-maps-foliage and @fig-bar-foliage-continent: while Deciduous Broadleaf and Evergreen Broadleaf appeared to occupy similar geographical ranges at the continent level, this ridge plot shows they are only partially overlapping in latitude. Evergreen Broadleaf is the only foliage type with a substantial tropical presence, while Deciduous Broadleaf, like both needleleaf types, remains overwhelmingly concentrated in the temperate Northern Hemisphere. This confirms that latitude (more than continental identity) is the primary driver structuring the geographical distribution of foliage types in this dataset, consistent with ecological expectations linking foliage strategy to climate.

## Taxonomic richness by continent

This subsection turns from the spatial and climatic distribution of foliage types to a different question: "how much taxonomic diversity does each continent actually contain ?" This question, however, cannot be answered directly by simply counting the number of distinct species or genera observed per continent, precisely because of the sampling imbalance identified in the first subsection of this report. A continent with more observations is mechanically more likely to have recorded more distinct taxa, even if its underlying biodiversity is not necessarily higher. Comparing raw taxonomic counts between continents therefore risks conflating genuine biodiversity differences with differences in sampling effort alone.

Three complementary views are used to address this issue. @tbl-taxa-continent first reports the raw number of distinct taxa recorded per continent, providing a simple numerical summary of the dataset's taxonomic content. @fig-richness-continent then visualizes these same raw counts as a bar chart, making it easier to compare continents at a glance, while keeping in mind that, at this stage, these values remain directly influenced by each continent's sampling volume, as shown in @fig-bar-continent. Finally, @fig-rarefaction addresses this limitation directly through rarefaction curves, which estimate the expected number of unique species as a function of sample size, allowing continents to be compared on an equal footing regardless of how many observations were actually collected for each.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-taxa-continent
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| tbl-cap: "Table of the taxonomic richness by continent"
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| tbl-width: 14
#| tbl-height: 10
#| tbl-align: center


tableau_taxons <- df %>%
  filter(!is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarise(
    Foliage = n_distinct(level0),
    Families = n_distinct(level1_family),
    Genus   = n_distinct(level2_genus),
    Species  = n_distinct(level3_species),
    Complete_taxons = n_distinct(paste(
      level1_family,
      level2_genus,
      level3_species,
      sep = "_"
    )),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


kable(tableau_taxons)

```

```{r}
#| label: fig-richness-continent
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Taxonomic richness by continent (raw values)"
#| fig-cap-location: bottom
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-align: center


richness <- df %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarise(
    n_families      = n_distinct(level1_family),
    n_genera        = n_distinct(level2_genus),
    n_species       = n_distinct(level3_species),
    n_observations  = n()
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    families_100obs = round(n_families / n_observations * 100, 1),
    genera_100obs   = round(n_genera   / n_observations * 100, 1),
```
